The US Treasury Department has issued fresh sanctions aimed at penalising Iran's energy sector [Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
The United States has launched another wave of sanctions against Iran under its Operation Economic Outcast, a move that comes shortly after US President Donald Trump threatened renewed military action next year.
The Department of the Treasury announced on Monday that it had targeted more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel with sanctions “in a sweeping effort to disrupt Iran’s global shadow banking networks”.

“Iran’s shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime,” said US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.
The US Treasury claimed these entities help Iran “move billions of dollars through the international financial system to provide the regime access to foreign currency despite comprehensive sanctions”.
Bessent also vowed the “Treasury will continue dismantling these illicit networks until we have buried the head of the snake.”
The Central Bank of Iran oversees the designated entities, according to the statement.

Several state attorneys general have announced investigations into Grok in recent months [File: Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters]By AP and ReutersPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
The US states of Virginia and Oregon have sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, saying the business harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when it designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images.
The attorneys general of both states filed complaints in separate lawsuits on Monday.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Dutch court bans xAI’s Grok from generating nonconsensual nude imageslist 2 of 4Musk’s Grok accused of violating Canadian privacy laws on deepfakeslist 3 of 4xAI sues user for exploiting AI tool to sexualise minorslist 4 of 4‘Just ask Grok’: How ISIL is using Big Tech’s AI to build bombsend of list
Several states had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue.
The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode”. The feature allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.
The company prioritised its business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”

By Evan Semones and Eva McKendPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.
The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump proposes new rules to ban gender-affirming care for transgender youthlist 2 of 3Failure of rival health bills underscores impasse in US politicslist 3 of 3Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies amid historic US measles resurgenceend of list
“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”
Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.
Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.
‘Every spare dime’ needed for medications
Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.

Parastoo Ahmadi and her production team were flogged for 'offending public decency' after the singer appeared without a hijab [File: AP/ Vahid Salemi]By AFP and ReutersPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
Iran has flogged a singer and her production team after they were convicted of “offending public decency”, according to local media.
The sentence of 74 lashes handed down to Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team was carried out in the city of Qom on Monday, the singer’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Emtedad news website.

A court in the city had sentenced the quintet in June. They were convicted of “producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online” over a video showing Ahmadi performing without wearing the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians.
The video was posted on YouTube in December 2024. In addition to the flogging, the five were banned for two years from taking part in artistic and musical activities and leaving Iran.
Western governments and human rights groups have condemned flogging as a form of torture that violates international law.
Iran rejects criticism of its human rights record and says Western countries should address abuses of their own.
Iran’s mandatory hijab rules became a focal point of protests in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish Iranian woman, died in custody following her arrest for allegedly violating the dress code.

Residents have been warned of the danger, and police have been stationed on roads leading into and out of Zekeriyakoy, the neighbourhood north of Istanbul where surveillance cameras have spotted the lion [File: Reuters]By AFP and APPublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
Police and animal welfare teams have launched a hunt for a lioness reported to be prowling the outskirts of Istanbul.
City authorities closed a woodland area in the northern Sariyer district on Monday as the teams expanded a search for the big cat, which was spotted in the area the previous evening.

Turkiye’s National Parks Directorate said on Sunday that police officers in Zekeriyakoy, north of Istanbul’s European side, had reported spotting “an animal resembling a lion” on surveillance cameras.
Grainy security camera footage republished by Turkish media appeared to show what looked like a big cat prowling across a patch of open countryside.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gul’s office confirmed the information, saying that “the necessary care is being taken to capture it alive”.
The parks authority said specialist veterinarians and teams equipped with thermal imaging cameras were assisting in the search.
More than 70 personnel, supported by drones, were searching in and around the nearby Belgrade Forest, which covers 54 square kilometres (21 square miles) north of Istanbul.
Local resident Arda Koc said he saw the lioness after joining the search on Sunday evening.

Garment workers have been protesting in recent weeks over demands for an increase in minimum wages [File: Abu Sufian Jewel/AFP]By Caolán MageePublished On 23 Nov 202623 Nov 2026
Representatives of Bangladeshi garment workers have rejected a pay offer from employers.
Factory owners submitted a pay proposal at a meeting convened by the government-appointed wage board on Monday, but worker representatives dismissed it as too low.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4Gaza mourns UNRWA worker killed in Israeli strikelist 2 of 4Israeli strikes kill at least three, including UNRWA worker, in Gazalist 3 of 4Why did COP31 climate talks collapse without a deal?list 4 of 4Tajikistan moves to leave ICC amid US push against courtend of list
The failure to reach an agreement during the wage talks suggests that the weeks of strikes and protests over the minimum wage in the industry could persist.
Babul Akhter, who represents workers on the wage board, told reporters after the meeting that “the offer … falls far short of what we have been demanding”, according to the AFP news agency.
The board kept the figure that had been offered confidential, although Chairman Judge Syed Azad Subhani said the proposed monthly minimum wage was above 14,500 taka ($116).
Workers’ representatives had formally proposed 32,000 taka ($258) for the lowest regular pay grade and 30,000 taka ($241) for apprentices.
Bangladesh’s garment industry brings in about $38bn a year, employs around four million people, and accounts for roughly four-fifths of the country’s export earnings.

United States President Donald Trump has ordered the military to delay a planned controlled detonation of more than four tonnes of explosives in the Midwestern state of Iowa until a federal appeals court and the state’s governor sign off on it.
Trump’s announcement on Monday comes amid a string of delays and a late-stage legal challenge raised by environmental groups in Iowa over approximately 9,700 pounds of degraded lead azide stored in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near the city of Middletown.
